She did not turn, but her shoulders gave a little shrug under the thin wool of her shawl. "Nothin', James. Just the same grey buildings, and the same grey sky." She sighed, a small, weary sound that pained him more than any cry. "I was just thinkin' how the fields must look now at home, with the first green showin' through." "We'll see them again, dear," he said, coming to stand behind her. "It won't be forever we're in this place." "Forever's a long time," she whispered, and she turned to him at last, her eyes looking too large for her pale face. "I'm so tired of mending, James. My fingers ache, and Mrs. Gable says my stitches ain't fine enough. She says I'll never earn my keep if I don't take more care." A single tear traced a path down her cheek. "Oh, hush now," he said, taking her small, reddened hand in his own. "You take all the care in the world. 'Tis the light that's poor, and the thread that's coarse. That ain't your fault, Clara." He led her away from the window, to the little stool beside the hearth where a meager fire struggled for life. He had spent his last few pennies on a small scuttle of coal that morning, for the damp chill of their attic room seemed to seep into his sister's very bones. "What would you do, if you did not have to mend?" he asked, trying to draw her out of her sadness. She looked into the flickering flames, a little spark of life returning to her own gaze. "I would draw," she said softly. "I'd draw the lane at home, with the big oak tree, and the stream behind the cottage. I'd make the sky so blue, and the grass so green, you'd think you could smell the clover, James." He watched her, his heart a heavy weight in his chest. He knew what this meant. He had a book, a heavy leather-bound volume of poetry his father had given him, the only thing of real value he had carried with him from their broken home. It was his treasure; in the lonely evenings, its verses were his only company. Rising, he went to the small trunk in the corner of the room. "I have an errand to run, Clara," he said, his back to her. "Will you be alright for a short while?" "Where are you going, James?" "Just to the bookseller's on the corner. I have a query for him." He did not dare to look at her as he wrapped the book in a bit of spare cloth and tucked it under his arm. He could not bear for her to see the truth in his eyes, nor for her to protest. Mr. Alport, the bookseller, was a stern man with spectacles perched on the end of his nose. He took the book and turned it over and over in his hands. "A fine binding," he allowed, "but the pages are foxed. Poetry, you say? There is not much call for poetry these days, young man." James's heart sank. "It was my father's," he said, his voice quiet. As the paper fell away, she gave a little gasp. She lifted one of the pencils, a brilliant, perfect blue, and held it as if it were a jewel. "Oh, James," she said, and her voice broke. "Oh, James, you shouldn't have." "There's paper too, dear," he said, his own throat tight. "You can draw the stream, and the big oak tree." She looked from the pencils to his face, and in the dim light she saw the space on the little shelf where his book had always stood. "You are the best brother in all the world," she cried into his shoulder, "the very best." And James, holding his little sister, felt that the price he had paid was a very small one indeed.

"That is all for now," he answered gently, closing the door. "But it is a great deal, is it not? See how the fire burns; we shall not be cold again to-night."
He drew the calico settee nearer to the hearth, and made her sit, taking the place beside her. For a while they were silent, listening to the hissing of the wood and the distant, unfamiliar clamour of the city. The raw dampness had fled the little room, replaced by a dry, companionable heat that began to soothe Winnie's chilled frame.
"I am hungry, Governor," she said at last, leaning her head against his shoulder.
"Are you? Then we shall have a feast."
He rose and went to the other closet, the one he had called Mother Hubbard's cupboard. It was scarcely better stocked than its namesake's, but Winthrop brought forth a loaf of bread, a small pot of butter, and a tin of tea with an air of satisfaction. From a peg he took a little kettle, and after fetching water from a pump in the entry, he set it amongst the coals to boil. Winnie watched his every movement, her quietness a sign of fatigue rather than her recent fretfulness. The simple, methodical tasks seemed to calm her as much as they did him.

"It is a very good supper, Winthrop," she declared, taking her last sip.
"I am glad you think so, little sister."

Winnie looked to her brother for permission. At his nod, she slipped off the settee and went to the woman's side.
"What is your name, little one?"
"Winnie, ma'am."
"Winnie. That is a sweet name for a sweet little face," said Mrs. Nettley, gently touching the child's pale cheek. "You look tired to the bone, poor lamb. This big city is a noisy, weary place after the country, I'll be bound."
"Yes, ma'am," Winnie whispered, her heart warming to this unexpected tenderness.
"Well, you have a good brother to look after you; there is no better young man in all Mannahatta than Mr. Landholm, though I say it myself. Now, you drink this broth while it's hot. It will help you sleep."

He laid her down and gently removed her shoes.
"Will you be alright, Winnie?" he asked softly.
"Yes," she said, already half-asleep. "It is a nice room, Winthrop. Good night."

He thought of his father's letter, and the words that had been written with such weary resignation; "I guess I'll take Asahel and go to the West." The farm, the home of his boyhood, with its green fields and familiar woods, was to be sold to pay a debt incurred for him. The thought was a bitter one. He had come to Mannahatta to make his fortune, to be a help and not a burden to his family; and yet, after years of toil, he had barely enough to keep himself, let alone to send anything home. And now he had Winnie.

He thought of the food, the rent for this larger space, the hundred small necessities that a sick child required. His purse was nearly empty. He would have to find more work, any kind of work, and quickly. He was a clerk, and a good one; but clerks were plentiful, and positions few. A sense of his own powerlessness washed over him, a feeling as chill and raw as the spring air had been that afternoon. He bowed his head in his hands, not in despair, but in a deep and troubled prayer. His strength was not his own; he knew that well. It came from a higher source, and to that source he must look now.

Below was a small, paved courtyard, cluttered with barrels and boxes. A woman was shaking a rug from a window opposite, and a large grey cat sat on a wall, washing its face with an air of immense indifference. There were no trees, no grass, not a single green thing in sight. A wave of homesickness washed over her so powerful it made her feel dizzy.
She turned from the window and went into the other room. Winthrop was not there, but a good fire was burning, and the kettle was singing on the hob. A plate with a covered cloth sat on the table. Under it, she found a fresh roll and a small piece of cheese. He had thought of her breakfast before he left. A little note, written in his clear, strong hand, was propped against the plate. "I have gone to seek work," it read. "I will not be long. Be a good girl for your Governor."
She ate her breakfast slowly, sitting on the settee and staring at the fire. The little room felt very empty without him. The city noises seemed louder, more threatening. Her old enemy, fretfulness, began to stir within her. She felt a strong inclination to cry, but the tears would not come. Instead, a restless energy took hold of her. She wandered around the room, touching things; Winthrop's few books on their small shelf, the smooth wood of the mantelpiece, the rough texture of the calico settee. She looked again into the wood-closet, as if hoping to find something new. She opened the door to his "storehouse" and peered inside, but the few simple provisions on the shelves held no interest for her.

A drayman was shouting at his horses, which had become entangled in their traces. A boy with a basket of rolls was calling out his wares in a high, clear voice. It was all noise and hurry and confusion. Winnie felt a great longing for the quiet of the woods at Shahweetah, for the familiar, gentle murmur of the brook.
"I hate it here," she whispered to the grimy windowpane. "I want to go home."
But home was gone. The word had no meaning anymore. There was only this room, and Winthrop. And he had left her. The thought brought a lump to her throat. She pressed her forehead against the cool glass and closed her eyes.
How long she stood there, she did not know; but she was roused by a sound in the room behind her. She turned, her heart leaping with the thought that it was Winthrop returned. But the man standing in the doorway was a stranger. He was young, not much older than her brother, with a pleasant, rather dreamy face and a smudge of blue paint on his cheek. It was George Nettley.
"I do beg your pardon," he said, looking as startled as she. "I knocked, but there was no answer. I was looking for Mr. Landholm."
Winnie found her voice. "He is not here. He has gone out."
"Oh. I see." He lingered in the doorway, seeming at a loss for what to do next. His eyes, which were a bright, observant blue, took in the room, the fire, and Winnie herself, standing small and forlorn by the window. "You must be his sister, Winnie."
She nodded.
"My mother told me you had arrived. I am George Nettley. We live downstairs."
He had a sketchbook in his hand, and he shifted it from one hand to the other. "I hope the city is not too loud for you," he said, with a shy smile. "It takes some getting used to."
"It is very loud," Winnie said, her lip trembling slightly. "And there are no trees."
"No," he agreed, his expression sympathetic. "Not many down here by the docks. But there are other things. You just have to know where to look." He took a step into the room. "Look here," he said, coming to stand beside her at the window. He pointed down into the street. "You see that man there, selling the oysters from his cart? See the way the steam rises from his pot? Winnie looked. She had seen only a crowd of drab, hurrying people. But now, guided by his words, she began to see the details; the flash of colour, the curl of steam, the sharp, dark shadow cast by the corner of a building. It was like a picture, she thought, a very busy, complicated picture.
"And the ships," George went on, his initial shyness forgotten in his enthusiasm. "Have you seen the ships? Their masts are a whole forest, right at the end of the street. A forest without leaves, to be sure, but a forest nonetheless."
He opened his sketchbook. On the page was a half-finished drawing of a ship's rigging, a beautiful, intricate web of lines and ropes against a pale sky. Winnie stared at it, fascinated. She had never seen anything like it.
"Did you draw that?" she asked, her voice full of awe.
"I did," he said. "It's my work. Or my pleasure, at any rate. My mother hopes I will become a portrait painter, for it pays better; but I would rather draw ships and streets all day." He smiled at her again. "Perhaps one day, when you are feeling stronger, your brother will let me take you to see them. The big ships that sail to England and beyond."
The idea was so grand, so exciting, that Winnie for a moment forgot her homesickness entirely. "Truly?"
"Truly."
At that moment, they heard Winthrop's step on the stair. He came in looking tired, but his face lit up when he saw Winnie was not alone, and that she was smiling.
"Mr. Nettley," he said, shaking the young artist's hand. "I am glad to see you. I hope my little sister has not been too much trouble."
"Not at all, not at all," said George cheerfully. "We have been discovering the artistic treasures of Little South St. I have just been promising to show her the ships' masts."
"That is a promise you must keep," said Winthrop, putting a hand on Winnie's shoulder. He could feel that the rigid, unhappy tension had gone out of her small frame. He looked from his sister's animated face to the kind, paint-smudged face of his neighbour, and a feeling of profound gratitude filled his heart. He was not alone in his watch. There were others who would help to tend his fragile vine.
"I found no work today," he told her quietly, after George had gone. "But I am not discouraged. We will manage, Winnie."
"I know we will, Governor," she said, leaning against him. "Mr. George says there is a forest at the end of our street."
Winthrop looked down at her, puzzled.
"A forest of masts," she explained, her eyes shining. "He is going to take us to see it."
Winthrop smoothed her hair back from her forehead. The shadows had not fled away; they were still there, dark and pressing. The mortgage, the rent, the future, all lay in wait. But for today, for this one moment, a little light had broken through. And for a boy who had to be a man, and a brother who had to be a world, that was enough.

"Truly."

He sought a clerkship, a position in a counting house, any employment where his good hand and educated mind might be of use. He presented himself at warehouses and shipping offices, his clothes neat, his manner composed; but the city was full of young men like him, and work was a prize not easily won.

Winnie would be waiting for him on the settee, a book in her lap that she had not the heart to read, her eyes fixed upon the door. He sat by her side long after she had fallen into a restless sleep, his hand on her forehead, his mind a turmoil of doubt and fear. He did not complain; he did not slow his pace. He simply worked.

A future that now seemed a mocking phantom.

He had come to the city to make his fortune, to be a help to his family. Instead, he was hauling barrels like an animal for a pittance, while the home he had left behind crumbled into ruin. He sat there for a long time, the lamp flickering, casting long, dancing shadows on the wall. The city murmured outside, a vast, indifferent beast. He felt utterly, terribly alone. The small moment of light that Winnie's "forest of masts" had brought seemed a lifetime ago, a child's fantasy in a brutal, unforgiving world.

Slowly, he raised his head. He looked at the closed door of Winnie's room. He could hear her stir in her sleep, a soft sigh. She was his charge. She was his world. For her, he had to be strong. For her, he had to endure. The humiliation, the pain, the despair -- they were his to bear, so that she might have a space to breathe, a place of peace.

He folded the letter and put it away. He would not tell her. He would not tell anyone. He would rise in the morning, and his body would ache, and he would go back to the docks. He would earn his few cents a barrel. It was not enough. It would never be enough to save the farm. But it was enough for today. It was enough for tomorrow's bread, and for a stick of wood for the fire. It was all he had.

He blew out the lamp and stood in the darkness, looking towards the window where the first faint, grey light of another day was beginning to outline the rooftops. The shadows had not fled away; they had grown darker, longer, and more menacing than ever before. But Winthrop Landholm, his hands raw and his heart aching, stood to face them. He was a sturdy tree, and the storm was breaking over him. He would not, he could not, fall.

He would earn his few cents a barrel. It was not enough. It would never be enough to save the farm. But it was enough for today. It was enough for tomorrow's bread, and for a stick of wood for the fire. It was all he had.

He blew out the lamp and stood in the darkness, looking towards the window where the first faint, grey light of another day was beginning to outline the rooftops. The shadows had not fled away; they had grown darker, longer, and more menacing than ever before. But Winthrop Landholm, his hands raw and his heart aching, stood to face them. He was a sturdy tree, and the storm was breaking over him. He would not, he could not, fall.

"I will not, sir."

The faces of the passers-by no longer seemed critical, but part of a great, bustling human family of which he was, at last, a functioning member. He had a place. He had a purpose. He was Winthrop Landholm, assistant to Mr. Anstice, the bookseller.

It was a wild extravagance, but his heart felt expansive enough for it.

"Governor! You are back! What happened? Tell me!"

"I have the place, Winnie," he said at last, his voice quiet. "I am to be a bookseller's assistant."

"Oh, Winthrop! I knew it! I knew you would!" she cried, her arms tightening around his neck. "Is it a good place? Is it warm? Will they be kind to you?"

"It is the best place in the world, I think," he said, laughing a little at her torrent of questions. "It is full of books from the floor to the ceiling. And it is warm. And the gentleman, Mr. Anstice, is a good man, I think, though very particular. And look what I have brought to celebrate."

He produced the little paper bag from his coat pocket. Winnie's eyes widened. "Cakes! Oh, Governor, you shouldn't have! We must be so careful."

"Today we need not be careful," he said, his heart full. "Today we have a victory."

They sat together by the fire, on the little calico settee, and ate the cakes. They were a simple treat, but to them they tasted like the most luxurious of feasts. Winnie chattered happily, asking a hundred questions about the shop and Mr. Anstice and what Winthrop would have to do, her face animated with a joy he had not seen on it for so long.

He answered all her questions, describing the dusty, quiet haven, the stern but just old man, and the promise of work that would engage his mind. As he spoke, he felt the last of the deep, weary ache leave his bones, the ache that had come not just from the labour at the docks, but from the hopelessness that had accompanied it.

The little room was quiet, filled with the soft sounds of his sister's breathing from the next room and the faint, distant hum of the city. He looked around him; at the worn furniture, the bare floors, the little closet that held their meager supplies. It was still a poor and humble shelter. The mortgage on the farm still loomed. His father's future was still uncertain. Many shadows remained.

But now, a steady light had been kindled against them. It was not a bonfire, but a single, well-tended lamp, and by its light, he could see the path ahead. He bowed his head, and in the quiet of the little attic, with a heart overflowing with gratitude, he gave thanks. Tomorrow, he would begin again.

He looked around him; at the worn furniture, the bare floors, the little closet that held their meager supplies. It was still a poor and humble shelter. The mortgage on the farm still loomed. He bowed his head, and in the quiet of the little attic, with a heart overflowing with gratitude, he gave thanks. Tomorrow, he would begin again.

He thought of his father's weary sigh, of the mortgage, of the long, hard road. What was the use of saving a farm if he could not save his sister?

He sank to his knees by the window, his head bowed. He did not pray with words. His whole being was a prayer, a desperate, silent plea sent up into the dark, indifferent sky. The pilgrim had stumbled. He had fallen. And he did not know if he had the strength to rise. The night was very long, and the dawn seemed a thing of impossibility. The shadows had not fled away; they had gathered in his own small room, and in his heart.
